description: We are Quantum Copper, an innovative tech team from Antofagasta, Chile—heart of the Atacama Desert and a global hub for astronomy and extreme environments. We are building Tailings & Waste SAR-Guard, a NISAR, Sentinel-1, and ground-robotics early-warning system detecting ground deformation and seepage to protect citizens near landfills and tailings dams like María Elena. Our strength combines software, satellite data analysis, and problem-solving inspired by northern Chile's resilience.
summary: VIGÍA Norte is an orbit-to-ground geotechnical screening system built for the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge to protect communities and help municipalities and small mining operators prioritize field inspections around tailings dams and leach-residue piles in northern Chile's Atacama Desert. Anchored by free NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band backscatter (L2 GCOV) and soil moisture (L3 SME2) data—and complemented by ESA Sentinel-1 C-band radar, auxiliary optical/DEM datasets, and a Chilean seismic ground-motion model (Montalva et al., 2017)—the system compares surrounding rings (0–500 m and 500–1000 m) against a natural control zone, then deploys a Yahboom ROSMASTER wheeled robot equipped with a Raspberry Pi and Orbbec RGB-D depth camera for on-site verification. Tested on November 15 polygons at María Elena's leach-residue pile—right beside the town—and the Talabre tailings dam, VIGÍA Norte delivers transparent, uncertainty-calibrated alerts.
details:
Project details

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

VIGÍA Norte turns free radar data from NASA and ISRO's NISAR into a short, prioritized list of places to inspect around mining waste deposits (tailings dams and leach-residue piles) in northern Chile. It does not try to predict failures: it simply tells a small operator or a municipality where to look first, and leaves the decision to a competent person.

  1. Data: we use NISAR L2 GCOV L-band backscatter (HH and HV, 20 m, track 097, frame 100) from 20 June, 6 October and 30 October 2026 (the main pair is 20 June → 6 October, with the same processing version; the 30 October image is a different version and is used for information only), and NISAR L3 SME2 soil moisture (200 m, provisional product) for seven dates between June and October 2026. Products are clipped to each site and worked in UTM 19S. The input data package is frozen with SHA-256 checksums. The robot operations platform also computes, as context only, Sentinel-2 indices and Copernicus DEM terrain; no result of this work depends on them.
  2. Change detection: we apply a speckle filter, compute the log-ratio between two passes of the same product version, and standardize it against a stable natural-terrain control zone 3–5 km away, like the control group of an experiment. The test is two-sided, because over saline tailings moisture can darken the radar signal instead of brightening it.
  3. Where we look: changes inside a deposit are mostly part of normal operation, so the system watches two rings around it (0–500 m and 500–1000 m), where water, displaced material or seepage could surface.
  4. Points to review: a cluster of changed pixels becomes a "review priority" point (yellow) only if it is larger than what the control zone produces by chance, keeping about one expected false alarm per site at most. A variogram of the control zone (the noise is local, with a range of about 200 m at María Elena) supports that minimum size.
  5. Verification: a person reviews each point in high-resolution imagery (photointerpretation) and fills in an opinion form. The algorithm never declares "high risk": only the human assessment does. For field inspection we designed a Yahboom ROSMASTER wheeled robot, with a Raspberry Pi and an Orbbec RGB-D camera, teleoperated from our ROB-HEART-O.1 platform (one operator at a time, 0.1 m/s maximum, emergency stop, no automatic dispatch). The live camera image already reaches the platform on the team's PC; it has not yet been tested in the field. The camera's depth is not used for measurement. Labels from future inspections would be used to recalibrate the threshold (future work).
  6. Earthquakes: a Chilean ground-motion model (Montalva et al., 2017), run with OpenQuake, estimates whether a recent earthquake shook a deposit hard enough to justify a review between radar passes. It is a complement and is not combined numerically with the radar.

RESULTS SO FAR

At the María Elena leach-residue pile, the surrounding rings changed 4.8 times more than the control zone in HH (95% CI 2.6–8.8, calibrated) and 13.4 times more in HV (95% CI 8.1–22.1). When the same rings were translated to 29 desert locations with no deposit, they produced 0 to 3 points, against 23 at the real deposit (empirical p ≈ 0.033). The change is largest next to the edge and decreases with distance. A person reviewed 12 of the 23 points in Google Earth: 10 are industrial infrastructure (plant, ponds, vats, roads) and only 2 are at the edge of the pile, so the excess change is not attributed to the pile. At the Talabre tailings dam the surroundings changed less than the control and no point appeared in any of the variants tested (with lower sensitivity). The results were stress-tested against threshold, polarization, filter size, outline errors of up to 100 m and robust statistics.

What we do not claim: the cause of the change is not confirmed (that is the job of the inspection), persistence cannot be evaluated with a single comparable pair, the rainfall analysis is pending, there was no field inspection, and the method cannot detect changes smaller than about 1 ha or weaker than about 0.5 dB. It is not real time: NISAR repeats every 12 days, so the analysis runs in batches with each pass.

BENEFITS

  • It uses open satellite data from NASA and ISRO, so the satellite information costs the user nothing.
  • It gives small and medium operators and municipalities, which normally have no continuous instrumentation, an objective and reproducible way to prioritize field inspections.
  • Every result carries its uncertainty and every step can be repeated: an independent verification script reproduces the figures (24 tests passed, 4 warnings and 0 failures).

EXPECTED IMPACT

Chile's registry lists hundreds of tailings deposits, many of them inactive or abandoned. Historical failure reviews point to water, accelerating deformation and earthquakes as the main triggers. VIGÍA Norte proposes a low-cost prioritization layer: every 12 days it can indicate which part of which deposit to visit first. After an earthquake, it adds an objective rule for deciding when to look again. The same workflow could be applied to any deposit within NISAR coverage by loading its outline. It still needs validation with field inspections.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

  • Python: h5py, rasterio, numpy, scipy, pandas, shapely, pyproj, OpenQuake engine.
  • Google Earth Pro to digitize deposit outlines and for photointerpretation.
  • ROB-HEART-O.1 web platform (interactive map, teleoperation and live robot image viewer). The NISAR layers are not deployed in the demonstration app: they are presented in the report and the presentation.
  • Robotics hardware: Yahboom ROSMASTER wheeled chassis (ROSMASTER X1 profile), Raspberry Pi, Yahboom motor controller board with Rosmaster_Lib.py through a CH340 USB-to-serial converter, Orbbec RGB-D camera, USB microphone and LED status display.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for literature search, code and technical writing, and optionally Ollama (local) for plain-language explanations inside the platform. Declared in the Space Apps AI section.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

The system links orbital L-band synthetic aperture radar monitoring with visual verification and a person's decision, and plans to close the loop down to the ground with a teleoperated robot. Instead of a fixed threshold, it calibrates every alarm against nearby natural terrain and tests itself with rings translated to places without deposits and with synthetic patches of known change. It also states precisely what it cannot see, which makes its alerts more trustworthy.

WHAT OUR TEAM TOOK INTO ACCOUNT

  • Keep a person in charge of every risk-related decision.
  • Declare every assumption and its uncertainty instead of overstating results.
  • Use only free and open data, so small operators can afford it.
  • A sound scientific basis, grounded in peer-reviewed literature on tailings-deposit failures, SAR change detection and Chilean seismology.
  • Choose sites the team knows: we are a team of mining engineering, civil engineering, computer science and architecture from Antofagasta.
